questions.question: $W=\operatorname{span}\{(1,0,0)^{\top},(0,1,0)^{\top}\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^3$, $\boldsymbol{b}=(1,1,1)^{\top}$. A student proposes $\boldsymbol{p}=(1,0,0)^{\top}\in W$, noting that $\boldsymbol{e}=\boldsymbol{b}-\boldsymbol{p}=(0,1,1)^{\top}$ satisfies $\boldsymbol{e}\cdot\boldsymbol{p}=0$. Is $\boldsymbol{p}$ the orthogonal projection of $\boldsymbol{b}$ onto $W$?
options: Yes: $\boldsymbol{p}\in W$ and the error is orthogonal to $\boldsymbol{p}$
No: the projection of $\boldsymbol{b}$ must have the same length as $\boldsymbol{b}$
No: $\boldsymbol{e}$ must be orthogonal to all of $W$, but $\boldsymbol{e}\cdot(0,1,0)^{\top}=1$
Yes: any $\boldsymbol{p}\in W$ with $\boldsymbol{p}\neq\boldsymbol{0}$ will do

questions.question: Let $W$ be a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^n$ (dot product). Every $\boldsymbol{b}$ splits uniquely as $\boldsymbol{b}=\boldsymbol{p}+\boldsymbol{e}$ with $\boldsymbol{p}\in W$, $\boldsymbol{e}\in W^\perp$; $\boldsymbol{p}=\operatorname{proj}_W\boldsymbol{b}=P\boldsymbol{b}$. Why is $\boldsymbol{p}$ the point of $W$ closest to $\boldsymbol{b}$?
options: Because $\|\boldsymbol{p}\|\le\|\boldsymbol{b}\|$, so $\boldsymbol{p}$ is the shortest vector
Because $\boldsymbol{p}$ is the longest vector of $W$ shorter than $\boldsymbol{b}$
Because $\boldsymbol{e}$ is orthogonal to $\boldsymbol{p}$, which fixes the distance

questions.question: Let $W$ be a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^n$ (dot product). Every $\boldsymbol{b}$ splits uniquely as $\boldsymbol{b}=\boldsymbol{p}+\boldsymbol{e}$ with $\boldsymbol{p}\in W$, $\boldsymbol{e}\in W^\perp$; $\boldsymbol{p}=\operatorname{proj}_W\boldsymbol{b}=P\boldsymbol{b}$. What does the matrix $I-P$ do?
options: It is the inverse of $P$, undoing the projection step
It is again the orthogonal projection onto $W$ itself
It projects orthogonally onto $W^\perp$, sending $\boldsymbol{b}$ to $\boldsymbol{e}$
It reflects $\boldsymbol{b}$ across the subspace $W$ of $\mathbb{R}^n$

questions.question: $P$ is an orthogonal projection matrix, so $P^2=P$ and $P^{\top}=P$. If $P\boldsymbol{v}=\lambda\boldsymbol{v}$ with $\boldsymbol{v}\neq\boldsymbol{0}$, why must $\lambda\in\{0,1\}$?
options: Because $P$ is symmetric, so all eigenvalues are $\pm1$

questions.question: The columns $\boldsymbol{q}_1,\dots,\boldsymbol{q}_k$ of the $n\times k$ matrix $Q$ ($k<n$) form an orthonormal basis of a subspace $W\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$. Which matrix is the orthogonal projection matrix onto $W$?

Project $\boldsymbol{b}=(2,3,1)^{\top}$ orthogonally onto the line spanned by $\boldsymbol{a}=(1,1,0)^{\top}$, using $\boldsymbol{p}=\frac{\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{b}}{\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{a}}\boldsymbol{a}$.

Project $\boldsymbol{b}=(4,0,2)^{\top}$ onto the line spanned by $\boldsymbol{a}=(1,1,1)^{\top}$; the projection is $\boldsymbol{p}=(2,2,2)^{\top}$. What is the distance from $\boldsymbol{b}$ to this line?

Which matrix is the orthogonal projection matrix $P=\frac{\boldsymbol{a}\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}}{\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{a}}$ onto the line spanned by $\boldsymbol{a}=(1,2)^{\top}$ in $\mathbb{R}^2$?
A square matrix is an orthogonal projection matrix iff $P^2=P$ and $P^{\top}=P$. Which of these matrices is an orthogonal projection matrix?
$P$ is the $5\times5$ orthogonal projection matrix onto a $3$-dimensional subspace $W\subseteq\mathbb{R}^5$. What is the trace of $P$?

$P$ is the orthogonal projection matrix onto a subspace $W\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$, and $\boldsymbol{b}=P\boldsymbol{b}+\boldsymbol{e}$ with $\boldsymbol{e}\in W^\perp$. Always $\|P\boldsymbol{b}\|\le\|\boldsymbol{b}\|$; when does equality hold?
options: Exactly when $\boldsymbol{b}$ is orthogonal to all of $W$
Always, as orthogonal projections preserve length
Exactly when $\boldsymbol{b}$ is a unit vector, $\|\boldsymbol{b}\|=1$

questions.question: For $W=\operatorname{Col}(A)$, the column space of an $n\times k$ matrix $A$, the formula $P=A(A^{\top}A)^{-1}A^{\top}$ requires full column rank. Why?
options: Otherwise $\operatorname{Col}(A)$ is not a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^n$
Otherwise $A^{\top}A$ is singular and has no inverse
Otherwise $A^{\top}A$ is not a square matrix
Otherwise the resulting $P$ is not symmetric

questions.question: The projection matrix onto the line spanned by $\boldsymbol{a}\neq\boldsymbol{0}$ is $P=\frac{\boldsymbol{a}\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}}{\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{a}}$. How does $P$ change if $\boldsymbol{a}$ is replaced by $c\boldsymbol{a}$ with $c\neq0$?

$W=\operatorname{span}\{\boldsymbol{a}_1,\boldsymbol{a}_2\}$ with $\boldsymbol{a}_1=(1,0,0)^{\top}$, $\boldsymbol{a}_2=(1,1,0)^{\top}$ (the $x_1x_2$-plane), and $\boldsymbol{b}=(1,2,3)^{\top}$. What is $\operatorname{proj}_W\boldsymbol{b}$?
Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$, $W=\operatorname{Col}(A)$ and $\boldsymbol{b}=(3,1,4)^{\top}$. Using $P=A(A^{\top}A)^{-1}A^{\top}$, what is $P\boldsymbol{b}$?

For $\boldsymbol{b}=(1,2,3)^{\top}$ and the line $W$ spanned by $(1,1,1)^{\top}$, $\boldsymbol{p}=(2,2,2)^{\top}$ and $\|\boldsymbol{e}\|=\sqrt{2}$. What is the distance from $\boldsymbol{b}$ to the point $\boldsymbol{w}=(3,3,3)^{\top}\in W$?

$A$ ($n\times k$) has full column rank and $B$ ($k\times k$) is invertible, so $A$ and $AB$ span the same $W$. Compare $P_1=A(A^{\top}A)^{-1}A^{\top}$ with $P_2$, the same formula with $AB$ in place of $A$.
options: They are equal: the factors of $B$ cancel
They differ by the scalar $\det B$

questions.question: $P$ is the $n\times n$ orthogonal projection matrix onto a subspace $W\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$. For which $W$ is $P$ invertible?
Project $\boldsymbol{b}=(3,0,3)^{\top}$ orthogonally onto the plane $W=\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon x_1-x_2+x_3=0\}$ in $\mathbb{R}^3$, whose normal is $\boldsymbol{n}=(1,-1,1)^{\top}$.

$P=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$ satisfies $P^2=P$, and its column space is the $x_1$-axis. For $\boldsymbol{b}=(0,1)^{\top}$, $P\boldsymbol{b}=(1,0)^{\top}$. Is $P\boldsymbol{b}$ the point of the $x_1$-axis closest to $\boldsymbol{b}$?
options: No: the closest point is $\boldsymbol{b}$ itself
